headings.title: Introduction to Sexual Dysfunctions and Nursing Implications
headings.content: Sexual dysfunction refers to a problem that prevents an individual or couple from experiencing satisfaction during any stage of the sexual response cycle. This cycle includes desire, arousal, orgasm, and resolution. In clinical practice across Nigerian health institutions, patients rarely present with a chief complaint of sexual dysfunction due to cultural taboos and religious sensitivities. Nurses must therefore recognize subtle clinical indicators, such as chronic pelvic pain, relationship strain, or vague somatic complaints. Building a therapeutic, non-judgmental rapport is the foundation of effective nursing care. Nurses protect patient dignity, maintain strict confidentiality, and normalize discussions surrounding sexual health during routine health assessments.

headings.title: Comprehensive Assessment and Sexual History Taking
headings.content:
Taking a sexual history requires a structured, sensitive approach. Many clinicians utilize frameworks like the **PLISSIT model** to guide the depth of intervention:

- **Permission**: Asking the patient for consent to discuss sexual health, which immediately lowers anxiety.
- **Limited Information**: Providing factual details regarding normal physiological aging or illness effects.
- **Specific Suggestions**: Offering targeted behavioral adjustments for mild dysfunctions.
- **Intensive Therapy**: Referring the patient to a specialized sex therapist or psychiatrist when deep-rooted trauma exists.

During assessment, nurses screen for medications, substance use, and changes in partner dynamics.

headings.title: Identifying Underlying Physical and Psychological Causes
headings.content:
Sexual dysfunctions are rarely isolated phenomena; they are classified as organic, psychological, or mixed. 

| Category | Common Etiologies | Clinical Indicators |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Organic** | Diabetes mellitus, hypertension, pelvic surgery, hormonal imbalances | Gradual onset, loss of nocturnal erections, systemic disease history |
| **Psychological** | Performance anxiety, depression, past trauma, religious guilt | Sudden onset, situational triggers, normal physiological responses during sleep |

Laboratory evaluations often include fasting blood glucose, lipid profiles, and total testosterone levels to rule out metabolic and endocrine deficits.

headings.title: Psychological Interventions and Sex Therapy
headings.content: When psychological factors drive dysfunction, talk therapy and structured behavioral exercises are paramount. **Sensate focus therapy**, developed by Masters and Johnson, is a classic behavioral intervention. It requires couples to touch and explore each other's bodies without demanding sexual intercourse or orgasm. This technique systematically reduces performance anxiety and teaches mindfulness of physical sensations. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is also employed to reframe negative thought patterns, body image anxieties, and catastrophic beliefs about sexual adequacy.

headings.title: Pharmacological Management and Medical Treatments
headings.content: Pharmacotherapy targets physiological components, particularly erectile dysfunction and hypoactive sexual desire. **Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors**, such as sildenafil, enhance nitric oxide-mediated smooth muscle relaxation in the corpora cavernosa. Nurses must educate patients that these medications require sexual stimulation to work and are strictly contraindicated with organic nitrates due to the risk of severe hypotension. For postmenopausal women experiencing dyspareunia due to vaginal atrophy, topical estrogen therapy restores mucosal elasticity and lubrication. Hormonal replacement is also considered for documented hypogonadism in men after cardiac clearance.

headings.title: Lifestyle Modifications and Patient Education
headings.content: Lifestyle factors heavily influence vascular and neurological pathways essential for sexual health. Nurses educate patients on cardiovascular risk reduction, including regular aerobic exercise, smoking cessation, and weight management. Alcohol abuse and recreational drug use frequently impair central nervous system arousal and hinder orgasm. Dietary counseling emphasizing balanced nutrition supports metabolic health. Additionally, nurses review current prescription profiles, as medications like certain antihypertensives and antidepressants frequently cause sexual side effects that patients suffer in silence unless directly addressed.

headings.title: Multidisciplinary Care and Referral Pathways
headings.content: Effective management of complex sexual dysfunctions requires a collaborative team approach. Nurses act as central coordinators who bridge the gap between primary care, urology, gynecology, psychiatry, and marital counselling. When physical interventions fail or psychological distress overwhelms the patient, timely referral is necessary. Nurses prepare patients by explaining what to expect during specialist consultations, reducing stigma and fear of the unknown. Documenting baseline functional scores and treatment responses ensures continuity of care across all disciplines.
